danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Efter alt, hvad Napoleon havde sagt til ham — de vredesudbrud og de sidste tørt udtalte ord: »Jeg vil ikke opholde Dem længere, general; De vil modtage mit brev« — følte Balasjov sig overbevist om, at Napoleon ikke ville ønske at se ham igen og endog ville undgå endnu et møde med ham, en fornærmet udsending, især da han havde været vidne til hans usømmelige vrede. Men til sin overraskelse modtog Balasjov gennem Duroc en indbydelse til at spise middag med kejseren den dag.
Bessières, Caulaincourt og Berthier var til stede ved middagen.

Napoleon mødte Balasjov muntert og elskværdigt. Han viste ikke det mindste tegn på forlegenhed eller selvbebrejdelse over sit udbrud den morgen, men forsøgte tværtimod at berolige Balasjov. Det var tydeligt, at han længe havde været overbevist om, at det var umuligt for ham at begå en fejl, og at alt, hvad han gjorde, var rigtigt — ikke fordi det stemte overens med nogen idé om ret og uret, men fordi det var ham, der gjorde det.

Kejseren var i fortræffeligt humør efter sin ridetur gennem Vilna, hvor folkeskarer begejstret havde hilst og fulgt ham. Fra alle vinduer i de gader, han red igennem, hang tæpper, flag og hans monogram, og de polske damer viftede med lommetørklæder til ham.

Ved middagen, hvor han havde placeret Balasjov ved sin side, behandlede Napoleon ham ikke blot elskværdigt, men opførte sig, som om Balasjov var en af hans egne hoffolk, en af dem der sympatiserede med hans planer og burde glæde sig over hans succes. Under samtalen nævnte han Moskva og spurgte Balasjov om den russiske hovedstad, ikke blot som en interesseret rejsende, der spørger om en ny by, han agter at besøge, men som om han var overbevist om, at Balasjov, som russer, måtte føle sig smigret over hans nysgerrighed.
»Hvor mange indbyggere er der i Moskva? Hvor mange huse? Er det sandt, at Moskva kaldes 'Det hellige Moskva'? Hvor mange kirker er der i Moskva?« spurgte han.
Og da han fik svaret, at der var mere end to hundrede kirker, bemærkede han:
»Hvorfor så mange kirker?«
»Russerne er meget fromme,« svarede Balasjov.
»Men et stort antal klostre og kirker er altid et tegn på et folks tilbageståenhed,« sagde Napoleon og vendte sig mod Caulaincourt for at få denne til at anerkende bemærkningen.
Balasjov vovede ærbødigt at modsige den franske kejser.
»Hvert land har sin egen karakter,« sagde han.
»Men ingen steder i Europa er der noget lignende,« sagde Napoleon.
»Jeg beder om forladelse, Deres Majestæt,« svarede Balasjov, »foruden Rusland er der Spanien, hvor der også er mange kirker og klostre.«

Dette svar fra Balasjov, der hentydede til franskmændenes seneste nederlag i Spanien, blev højt værdsat, da han fortalte om det ved Aleksandrs hof, men det blev ikke værdsat ved Napoleons middag, hvor det gik ubemærket hen.

De uinteresserede og rådvilde ansigter hos marskalerne viste, at de var i tvivl om, hvad Balasjovs tone antydede. »Hvis der er en pointe, ser vi den ikke, eller den er slet ikke vittig,« syntes deres udtryk at sige. Så lidt blev hans modsvar påskønnet, at Napoleon slet ikke lagde mærke til det og naivt spurgte Balasjov, gennem hvilke byer den direkte vej derfra til Moskva gik. Balasjov, der var på vagt hele middagen, svarede, at ligesom »alle veje fører til Rom,« fører alle veje til Moskva: der var mange veje, og »blandt dem vejen over Poltáva, som Karl den Tolvte valgte.« Balasjov rødmede uvilkårligt af glæde over dette rammende svar, men næppe havde han udtalt ordet Poltáva, før Caulaincourt begyndte at tale om den dårlige vej fra Petersborg til Moskva og om sine minder fra Petersborg.

Efter middagen gik de ind for at drikke kaffe i Napoleons arbejdsværelse, der fire dage forinden havde været kejser Aleksandrs. Napoleon satte sig ned, legede med sin Sèvres-kaffekop og vinkede Balasjov hen til en stol ved sin side.

Napoleon var i det velkendte humør efter middagen, som mere end nogen fornuftig årsag gør et menneske tilfreds med sig selv og tilbøjelig til at betragte alle som sine venner. Det forekom ham, at han var omgivet af mænd, der tilbad ham, og han var overbevist om, at også Balasjov, efter middagen, var hans ven og beundrer. Napoleon vendte sig mod ham med et venligt, omend let ironisk smil.

»Man fortæller mig, at dette er det værelse, kejser Aleksandr beboede? Mærkværdigt, ikke sandt, general?« sagde han, tydeligvis uden at tvivle på, at denne bemærkning ville behage hans tilhører, da den beviste hans, Napoleons, overlegenhed over Aleksandr.
Balasjov svarede ikke og bøjede tavst hovedet.

»Ja. For fire dage siden sad Wintzingerode og Stein og rådslog i dette værelse,« fortsatte Napoleon med det samme hånlige og selvsikre smil. »Hvad jeg ikke kan forstå,« fortsatte han, »er, at kejser Aleksandr har omgivet sig med mine personlige fjender. Det forstår jeg ikke... Har han ikke tænkt over, at jeg kan gøre det samme?« Og han vendte sig spørgende mod Balasjov, og tydeligvis førte denne tanke ham tilbage til morgenens vrede, der stadig var frisk i ham.

»Og lad ham vide, at det vil jeg gøre!« sagde Napoleon og rejste sig, idet han skubbede koppen fra sig med hånden. »Jeg jager alle hans slægtninge fra Württemberg, Baden og Weimar ud af Tyskland... Ja. Jeg jager dem ud. Lad ham forberede et asyl for dem i Rusland!«

Balasjov bøjede hovedet med en mine, der antydede, at han gerne ville bukke og gå, og kun lyttede, fordi han ikke kunne undgå at høre, hvad der blev sagt til ham. Napoleon lagde ikke mærke til dette udtryk; han behandlede Balasjov ikke som en udsending fra sin fjende, men som en mand, der nu fuldt ud var ham hengiven og måtte glæde sig over sin tidligere herres ydmygelse.

»Og hvorfor har kejser Aleksandr påtaget sig kommandoen over hærene? Hvad er meningen med det? Krig er mit fag, men hans opgave er at regere og ikke kommandere hære! Hvorfor har han påtaget sig et sådant ansvar?«

Napoleon tog igen sin snustobaksdåse frem, gik flere gange tavst frem og tilbage i værelset og trådte så pludselig og uventet hen til Balasjov, og med et let smil, lige så selvsikkert, hurtigt og ubesværet, som om han foretog sig noget, der ikke blot var vigtigt, men behageligt for Balasjov, løftede han hånden op til den fyrreårige russiske generals ansigt og tog ham blidt i øret, idet han kun smilede med læberne.
At få sit øre knebet af kejseren blev ved det franske hof betragtet som den største ære og nådesbevisning.

»Nå, tilbeder og hofmand hos kejser Aleksandr, hvorfor siger De ingenting?« sagde han, som om det var latterligt i hans nærværelse at være tilbeder og hofmand hos nogen anden end ham selv, Napoleon. »Er hestene klar til generalen?« tilføjede han med en let bøjning af hovedet som svar på Balasjovs buk. »Lad ham få mine, han har lang vej.«
Brevet, som Balasjov medbragte, var det sidste, Napoleon sendte til Aleksandr. Alle detaljer fra mødet blev meddelt den russiske hersker, og krigen begyndte...

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: After everything Napoleon had said to him — those bursts of anger and the last coldly spoken words: "I will detain you no longer, General; you shall receive my letter" — Balashev felt convinced that Napoleon would not wish to see him again and would even avoid another meeting with him, an insulted envoy, especially after he had witnessed Napoleon's unseemly outburst. But to his surprise, Balashev received through Duroc an invitation to dine with the Emperor that day.
Bessieres, Caulaincourt, and Berthier were present at that dinner.

Napoleon greeted Balashev cheerfully and warmly. He showed no sign of embarrassment or self-reproach on account of his outburst that morning. On the contrary, he tried to put Balashev at ease. It was evident that he had long been convinced it was impossible for him to make a mistake, and that in his mind whatever he did was right — not because it aligned with any idea of right and wrong, but simply because he did it.

The Emperor was in very good spirits after his ride through Vilna, where crowds of people had rapturously greeted and followed him. From all the windows of the streets through which he rode, rugs, flags, and his monogram were displayed, and the Polish ladies waved their handkerchiefs as they welcomed him.

At dinner, having placed Balashev beside him, Napoleon not only treated him warmly but behaved as if Balashev were one of his own courtiers, one of those who sympathized with his plans and ought to rejoice at his success. In the course of conversation he mentioned Moscow and questioned Balashev about the Russian capital — not merely as an interested traveler asks about a new city he intends to visit, but as if convinced that Balashev, as a Russian, must be flattered by his curiosity.
"How many inhabitants are there in Moscow? How many houses? Is it true that Moscow is called 'Holy Moscow'? How many churches are there in Moscow?" he asked.
And receiving the reply that there were more than two hundred churches, he remarked:
"Why such a large number of churches?"
"The Russians are very devout," replied Balashev.
"But a large number of monasteries and churches is always a sign of a people's backwardness," said Napoleon, turning to Caulaincourt for appreciation of this remark.
Balashev respectfully ventured to disagree with the French Emperor.
"Every country has its own character," said he.
"But nowhere in Europe is there anything like that," said Napoleon.
"I beg your Majesty's pardon," returned Balashev, "besides Russia there is Spain, where there are also many churches and monasteries."

This reply of Balashev's, which hinted at the recent defeats of the French in Spain, was much appreciated when he told it at Alexander's court, but was not much appreciated at Napoleon's dinner, where it passed unnoticed.

The disinterested and puzzled faces of the marshals showed that they were confused as to what Balashev's tone was implying. "If there's a point, we don't see it, or it's not at all witty," their expressions seemed to say. So little was his remark appreciated that Napoleon didn't notice it at all and naively asked Balashev through what towns the direct road from there to Moscow passed. Balashev, who was alert throughout the dinner, replied that just as "all roads lead to Rome," so all roads lead to Moscow: there were many roads, and "among them the road through Poltava, which Charles XII chose." Balashev involuntarily flushed with pleasure at the cleverness of this reply, but hardly had he uttered the word "Poltava" before Caulaincourt began talking about the terrible condition of the road from Petersburg to Moscow and his Petersburg memories.

After dinner they went to drink coffee in Napoleon's study, which four days before had been Emperor Alexander's. Napoleon sat down, toying with his Sevres coffee cup, and motioned Balashev to a chair beside him.

Napoleon was in that well-known after-dinner mood which, more than any reasoned cause, makes a man contented with himself and inclined to view everyone as his friend. It seemed to him that he was surrounded by people who adored him, and he felt sure that after his dinner, Balashev too was his friend and admirer. Napoleon turned to him with a pleasant, though slightly ironic, smile.

"They tell me this is the room the Emperor Alexander occupied? Strange, isn't it, General?" he said, obviously not doubting that this remark would please his listener, since it proved his, Napoleon's, superiority over Alexander.
Balashev made no reply and bowed his head in silence.

"Yes. Four days ago in this room, Wintzingerode and Stein were deliberating," continued Napoleon with the same mocking and self-confident smile. "What I can't understand," he went on, "is that the Emperor Alexander has surrounded himself with my personal enemies. That I do not... understand. Has he not considered that I might do the same?" and he turned inquiringly to Balashev, and this thought evidently brought him back to the anger of that morning, which was still fresh.

"And let him know that I will do it!" said Napoleon, rising and pushing his cup aside. "I'll drive all his Wurttemberg, Baden, and Weimar relatives out of Germany... Yes, I'll drive them out. Let him prepare a refuge for them in Russia!"

Balashev bowed his head with an air that said he would like to take his leave and was only listening because he had no choice. Napoleon didn't notice this expression; he treated Balashev not as an envoy from his enemy, but as a man now fully devoted to him who should rejoice at his former master's humiliation.

"And why has the Emperor Alexander taken command of the armies? What's the good of that? War is my profession, but his business is to reign, not to command armies! Why has he taken on such a responsibility?"

Again Napoleon brought out his snuffbox, paced several times up and down the room in silence, and then suddenly and unexpectedly went up to Balashev and, with a slight smile, as confidently, quickly, and simply as if he were doing something not merely important but pleasing to Balashev, raised his hand to the forty-year-old Russian general's face and, taking him by the ear, pulled it gently, smiling with his lips only.
To have one's ear pulled by the Emperor was considered the greatest honor and mark of favor at the French court.

"Well, admirer and courtier of the Emperor Alexander, why don't you say anything?" said he, as if it were ridiculous, in his presence, to be the admirer and courtier of anyone but himself, Napoleon. "Are the horses ready for the general?" he added, with a slight inclination of his head in reply to Balashev's bow. "Let him have mine — he has a long way to go!"
The letter taken by Balashev was the last Napoleon sent to Alexander. Every detail of the interview was communicated to the Russian monarch, and the war began...
